**Law of mass action** (section 12.4.2) : the rate of a chemical reaction at each instant is proportional to the product of concentration terms of all the reactants.

If the balanced chemical equation shows more than one molecule of a reactant, the concentration of that reactant is raised to a power equal to the number of its molecules in the balanced equation.

For example, for \(\mathrm{A} + \mathrm{B} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{C}\),

Rate \(\alpha\ [\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]\)

Introducing a proportionality constant \(k\),

Rate \(= k\,[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]\)

This is the **rate equation**, and \(k\) is the **rate constant** of the reaction. Concentrations are expressed in \(\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}\) and are written by putting the formula in square brackets.

For a general reversible reaction

\(a\mathrm{A} + b\mathrm{B} \rightleftharpoons c\mathrm{C} + d\mathrm{D}\)

the equilibrium constant with respect to concentration is (Eq. 12.5)

\(K_C = \dfrac{[\mathrm{C}]^c [\mathrm{D}]^d}{[\mathrm{A}]^a [\mathrm{B}]^b}\)

where the square brackets denote the **equilibrium** molar concentrations, in \(\mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\), and each is raised to the power of its coefficient in the balanced chemical equation.

The expression follows from the law of mass action: at equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal, so \(k_f [\mathrm{A}]^a[\mathrm{B}]^b = k_r [\mathrm{C}]^c[\mathrm{D}]^d\), and hence \(K_C = \dfrac{k_f}{k_r} = \dfrac{[\mathrm{C}]^c [\mathrm{D}]^d}{[\mathrm{A}]^a [\mathrm{B}]^b}\).

The value of \(K_C\) depends only on the temperature, and its unit is \((\mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}})^{\Delta n}\).

For \(\mathrm{A(g)} + \mathrm{B(g)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{C(g)} + \mathrm{D(g)}\), the equilibrium constant in terms of partial pressures is

\(K_P = \dfrac{P_{\mathrm{C}}\,P_{\mathrm{D}}}{P_{\mathrm{A}}\,P_{\mathrm{B}}}\)

For a mixture of ideal gases the partial pressure of a component is proportional to its concentration at constant temperature (section 12.4.4). From \(P_{\mathrm{A}}V = n_{\mathrm{A}}RT\),

\(P_{\mathrm{A}} = \dfrac{n_{\mathrm{A}}}{V}RT = [\mathrm{A}]RT\), and similarly \(P_{\mathrm{B}} = [\mathrm{B}]RT\), \(P_{\mathrm{C}} = [\mathrm{C}]RT\), \(P_{\mathrm{D}} = [\mathrm{D}]RT\).

Substituting,

\(K_P = \dfrac{[\mathrm{C}]RT \cdot [\mathrm{D}]RT}{[\mathrm{A}]RT \cdot [\mathrm{B}]RT}\)

\(\therefore K_P = \dfrac{[\mathrm{C}][\mathrm{D}]}{[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]} \times \dfrac{(RT)^2}{(RT)^2}\)

\(\therefore K_P = K_C \times (RT)^{2-2} = K_C (RT)^0\)

\(\therefore K_P = K_C\)

Here \(\Delta n\) = (moles of gaseous products) \(-\) (moles of gaseous reactants) \(= 2 - 2 = 0\), so the general result \(K_P = K_C (RT)^{\Delta n}\) (Eq. 12.7) reduces to \(K_P = K_C\) for this reaction.

Each concentration is raised to the power of its coefficient in the balanced equation, with products in the numerator and reactants in the denominator.

i. \(2\mathrm{SO_2(g)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{SO_3(g)}\)

\(K_c = \dfrac{[\mathrm{SO_3(g)}]^2}{[\mathrm{SO_2(g)}]^2\,[\mathrm{O_2(g)}]}\)

Here \(\Delta n = 2 - 3 = -1\), so the unit of \(K_c\) is \((\mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}})^{-1} = \mathrm{mol^{-1}\ dm^{3}}\).

ii. \(\mathrm{N_2O_4(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NO_2(g)}\)

\(K_c = \dfrac{[\mathrm{NO_2(g)}]^2}{[\mathrm{N_2O_4(g)}]}\)

Here \(\Delta n = 2 - 1 = +1\), so the unit of \(K_c\) is \(\mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\).

Section 12.7 of this chapter gives the following applications of the equilibrium constant.

**1. Prediction of the direction of the reaction (12.7.1).** The same ratio of concentrations, formed when the concentrations are not necessarily equilibrium ones, is the reaction quotient \(Q_C\). Comparing it with \(K_C\) tells which way the net reaction must go :

- if \(Q_C < K_C\), the reaction proceeds from left to right (forward), making more product;
- if \(Q_C = K_C\), the system is already at equilibrium and no net reaction occurs;
- if \(Q_C > K_C\), the reaction proceeds from right to left, making more reactant.

**2. To know the extent of the reaction (12.7.2).** The magnitude of \(K_C\) is directly proportional to the equilibrium concentrations of the products and inversely proportional to those of the reactants. A very high value \((K_C > 10^3)\) means the forward reaction is favoured and the reaction nearly goes to completion; a very low value \((K_C < 10^{-3})\) means only a small fraction of the reactants is converted and the reverse reaction is favoured.

**3. To calculate equilibrium concentrations (12.7.3).** Given \(K_C\) and the initial amounts, the composition of the equilibrium mixture can be calculated — as done in the chapter for the esterification of ethanoic acid with ethanol, and in Problem 12.5 for \(\mathrm{H_2} + \mathrm{I_2} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{HI}\).

**4. Link between chemical equilibrium and chemical kinetics (12.7.4).** Since \(K_C = \dfrac{k_f}{k_r}\), the equilibrium constant relates the rate constants of the forward and reverse reactions : a very large \(K_C\) means \(k_f \gg k_r\) and the reaction goes almost to completion, while \(K_C\) near one means comparable concentrations of reactants and products at equilibrium.

**Note :** the prediction of the direction of a reaction from \(Q_C\) and \(K_C\) makes no comment on the *time* required to attain equilibrium.

A change of pressure does **not** change the value of the equilibrium constant. \(K_C\) (and \(K_P\)) is **temperature dependent only** — the second characteristic listed in section 12.6 is that the equilibrium constant is temperature dependent, so \(K_C\) and \(K_P\) change only when the temperature changes.

What a change of pressure can change is the **position** of the equilibrium, not the constant. The chapter's summary table states it directly : for pressure, the position of equilibrium "changes if reaction involves change in number of moles", while the value of \(K_C\) shows "no change". For \(\mathrm{H_2(g)} + \mathrm{I_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{HI(g)}\), where the number of gas molecules is the same on both sides, the chapter notes that "there is no change in value of \(K_C\) during any change in pressure of the equilibrium reaction mixture", and the position does not move either.

The chapter also states the general rule : in all cases of a change in concentration, pressure, temperature or the presence of a catalyst, once the equilibrium has been re-established after the change, the value of \(K_C\) will be unaltered — the one exception being temperature, which does alter \(K_C\) itself (Table 12.2).

| Irreversible reaction | Reversible reaction |
|---|---|
| Proceeds only in a single direction, from reactants to products. | Proceeds in both directions simultaneously — a forward reaction from reactants to products and a reverse (backward) reaction from products to reactants. |
| Goes on until one of the reactants is exhausted, i.e. it goes to completion. | Does not go to completion; some reactant always remains along with the products. |
| Written with a single arrow \(\longrightarrow\) pointing towards the products. | Written with a double arrow \(\rightleftharpoons\), one arrow in each direction. |
| The products cannot be converted back into the reactants under the same conditions. | The products react back to re-form the reactants, so a state of equilibrium is reached. |
| Example : \(\mathrm{C(s)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CO_2(g)}\); also the decomposition of \(\mathrm{CaCO_3}\) in an **open** vessel, from which the \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) escapes so the \(\mathrm{CaCO_3}\) cannot be obtained back. | Example : \(\mathrm{H_2(g)} + \mathrm{I_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{HI(g)}\); also the decomposition of \(\mathrm{CaCO_3}\) in a **closed** vessel, where \(\mathrm{CaCO_3}\), \(\mathrm{CaO}\) and \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) are all present at constant concentrations. |

In the Haber process ammonia is made by the reversible reaction

\(\mathrm{N_2(g)} + 3\mathrm{H_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NH_3(g)} + \text{Heat}\)

which proceeds with a **decrease** in the number of moles \((\Delta n = -2)\) and is **exothermic** in the forward direction. The conditions are chosen from those two facts.

**Concentration.** Nitrogen and hydrogen are taken in the stoichiometric ratio \(1 : 3\) by volume (Fig. 12.6), the nitrogen from the air and the hydrogen from natural gas. Adding more \(\mathrm{N_2}\) or \(\mathrm{H_2}\) makes \(Q_C < K_C\), so the equilibrium shifts left to right and the added reactant is consumed, increasing the yield of \(\mathrm{NH_3}\). The ammonia formed is removed by cooling the gases until it liquefies, and the unreacted gases are recycled — removing a product likewise drives the forward reaction.

**Temperature.** Since the forward reaction is exothermic, lowering the temperature shifts the equilibrium to the right. But at a low temperature the rate of reaction is small and equilibrium takes too long, while at a high temperature the reaction is fast but the ammonia appreciably decomposes. An **optimum temperature** is therefore used, about **773 K**.

**Pressure.** The forward reaction proceeds with a decrease in the number of moles, so it is favoured by **high pressure**. At too high a pressure, however, the catalyst becomes inefficient, so an **optimum pressure** is used, about **250 atm**.

**Catalyst.** Iron containing a small quantity of molybdenum is used. It does not shift the equilibrium or change \(K_C\); it only lets equilibrium be reached faster.

*Note :* the labelled diagram of the plant in Fig. 12.6 marks slightly different working values — \(450\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and 200 atm — from the optimum values of about 773 K and about 250 atm given in the text of section 12.9. Either pair may be quoted; the reasoning behind them is the same.

A **reversible reaction** is one that proceeds in both directions at the same time : the forward reaction converts reactants into products and the reverse reaction converts products back into reactants. It is written with a double arrow, \(\rightleftharpoons\).

Because the reverse reaction exists, such a reaction never goes to completion in a closed system. As the forward reaction proceeds the reactants are used up, so its rate falls; as products accumulate the rate of the reverse reaction rises. Eventually **the two rates become equal**, and from that moment the concentrations of all the species stop changing. This is the state of equilibrium.

The equilibrium so reached is **dynamic**, not static. The reaction has not stopped — as the chapter puts it in section 12.4.3, "though the concentration ratio remains unchanged, both the forward as well as reverse reactions do proceed at equilibrium, but at the same rate. Therefore the chemical equilibrium is a dynamic equilibrium."

So the relation is this : **a reversible reaction in a closed system is the condition for a dynamic equilibrium, and the dynamic equilibrium is the state that reversible reaction finally settles into** — a state of constant measurable properties (concentration, pressure, density) maintained by two opposite reactions running at equal rates. An irreversible reaction has no reverse reaction and therefore cannot reach such a state; it simply runs until a reactant is exhausted.

\(\mathrm{BaSO_4(s)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{Ba^{2\oplus}(aq)} + \mathrm{SO_4^{2\ominus}(aq)}\)

This is a **heterogeneous** equilibrium. \(\mathrm{BaSO_4}\) is a pure solid, and by the rule of section 12.5.2 only the concentrations of gases and of dissolved (aq) substances appear in the equilibrium constant expression, so

\(K_C = [\mathrm{Ba^{2\oplus}(aq)}][\mathrm{SO_4^{2\ominus}(aq)}]\)

**a. Addition of \(\mathrm{Ba^{2\oplus}}\) ion.** The concentration of a species on the right is increased, so by Le Chatelier's principle the equilibrium shifts in the direction that consumes it, that is **backward, from right to left**. More \(\mathrm{BaSO_4}\) is precipitated and the concentration of \(\mathrm{SO_4^{2\ominus}}\) decreases.

**b. Removal of \(\mathrm{SO_4^{2\ominus}}\) ion.** A product has been removed, so the system reacts to replenish it and the equilibrium shifts **forward, from left to right**. More \(\mathrm{BaSO_4}\) dissolves.

**c. Addition of \(\mathrm{BaSO_4(s)}\).** **No effect on the position of the equilibrium.** \(\mathrm{BaSO_4}\) is a pure solid; the chapter notes that concentrations of pure solids do not change with the amount taken, which is why the solid does not appear in the expression for \(K_C\) at all. Adding more of it therefore alters neither \(Q_C\) nor the concentrations of the two ions.

In all three cases the **value** of \(K_C\) itself is unchanged — only the position of the equilibrium moves, and only in (a) and (b).

At equilibrium the concentrations of the reactants and the products stop changing, and the reaction *appears* to have stopped. It has not. Both the forward and the reverse reactions continue to occur, but **at equal rates**, so that whatever is consumed in one direction is produced at the same rate in the other and no net change is observed. This is what is meant by calling chemical equilibrium **dynamic**. Section 12.4.3 states it directly : "though the concentration ratio remains unchanged, both the forward as well as reverse reactions do proceed at equilibrium, but at the same rate. Therefore the chemical equilibrium is a dynamic equilibrium."

How it comes about (section 12.3 and Fig. 12.4) : at the start the rate of the forward reaction is high and the rate of the reverse reaction is very small. As the forward reaction proceeds the reactants are used up so its rate falls, while the products accumulate so the reverse rate rises. Finally the two rates become equal and equilibrium is established.

**Example.** Heat calcium carbonate strongly in a **closed** vessel :

\(\mathrm{CaCO_3(s)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CaO(s)} + \mathrm{CO_2(g)}\)

After some time the concentrations of \(\mathrm{CaCO_3}\), \(\mathrm{CaO}\) and \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) become constant and stay constant however long the experiment is continued at that temperature. The reaction looks as though it has stopped, but \(\mathrm{CaCO_3}\) is still decomposing and \(\mathrm{CaO}\) and \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) are still recombining, at the same rate — a dynamic equilibrium. (In an **open** vessel the \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) escapes, the reverse reaction cannot occur, and no equilibrium is reached.)

For a general gaseous reversible reaction

\(a\mathrm{A(g)} + b\mathrm{B(g)} \rightleftharpoons c\mathrm{C(g)} + d\mathrm{D(g)}\)

\(K_C = \dfrac{[\mathrm{C}]^c [\mathrm{D}]^d}{[\mathrm{A}]^a [\mathrm{B}]^b}\) and \(K_P = \dfrac{(P_{\mathrm{C}})^c (P_{\mathrm{D}})^d}{(P_{\mathrm{A}})^a (P_{\mathrm{B}})^b}\)

For an ideal gas the partial pressure of a component is proportional to its concentration at constant temperature : from \(P_{\mathrm{A}}V = n_{\mathrm{A}}RT\) we get \(P_{\mathrm{A}} = \dfrac{n_{\mathrm{A}}}{V}RT = [\mathrm{A}]RT\), and likewise for B, C and D.

Substituting these into \(K_P\),

\(K_P = \dfrac{[\mathrm{C}]^c (RT)^c\,[\mathrm{D}]^d (RT)^d}{[\mathrm{A}]^a (RT)^a\,[\mathrm{B}]^b (RT)^b}\)

\(\therefore K_P = \dfrac{[\mathrm{C}]^c [\mathrm{D}]^d}{[\mathrm{A}]^a [\mathrm{B}]^b} \times (RT)^{(c+d)-(a+b)}\)

\(\therefore K_P = K_C\,(RT)^{\Delta n}\) ....(12.7)

where \(\Delta n\) = (number of moles of gaseous products) \(-\) (number of moles of gaseous reactants) in the balanced chemical equation, and \(R\) is the molar gas constant.

**Consequences.**

- If \(\Delta n = 0\), \(K_P = K_C\). Example (Problem 12.3) : \(\mathrm{H_2(g)} + \mathrm{I_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{HI(g)}\).
- If \(\Delta n > 0\), \(K_P > K_C\).
- If \(\Delta n < 0\), \(K_P < K_C\). Example (Problem 12.2) : \(\mathrm{N_2(g)} + 3\mathrm{H_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NH_3(g)}\), where \(\Delta n = 2 - 4 = -2\) and \(K_P = K_C (RT)^{-2}\).

While calculating \(K_P\) the pressure should be expressed in bar, because the standard pressure is 1 bar.

**Statement (section 12.8).** Le Chatelier's principle states that when a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change in any of the factors determining the equilibrium conditions, the system will respond in such a way as to minimize the effect of the change. Equivalently : if a stress is applied to a reaction mixture at equilibrium, the reaction occurs in the direction which relieves the stress — a stress being any change in concentration, pressure, volume or temperature that disturbs the original equilibrium.

**1. Change in temperature.** In a reversible reaction the reverse reaction has an energy change equal and opposite to that of the forward reaction, so if one direction is exothermic the other is endothermic. Raising the temperature adds heat, and the stress is relieved by the direction that **absorbs** heat, i.e. the endothermic one; lowering the temperature favours the exothermic direction.

Example : \(\mathrm{PCl_5(g)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{PCl_3(g)} + \mathrm{Cl_2(g)} + 92.5\ \mathrm{kJ}\). The forward reaction is exothermic and the reverse endothermic, so an increase in temperature shifts the equilibrium in the reverse direction to use up the added heat.

Temperature is the one factor that also changes the **value** of the equilibrium constant. For \(\mathrm{CO(g)} + 2\mathrm{H_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_3OH(g)} + \text{Heat}\), Table 12.2 gives \(K_C = 1.7 \times 10^{17}\) at 298 K, \(1.1 \times 10^{11}\) at 500 K and \(2.1 \times 10^{6}\) at 1000 K : the forward reaction is exothermic, so raising the temperature shifts the position to the left and \(K_C\) decreases.

**2. Change in concentration.** If the concentration of one of the species in the equilibrium mixture is increased, the position of the equilibrium shifts in the direction that **consumes** that species; if a species is removed, it shifts in the direction that **replenishes** it. The equilibrium constant itself remains unchanged.

Example : \(\mathrm{N_2(g)} + 3\mathrm{H_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NH_3(g)} + \text{Heat}\), for which \(Q_C = K_C = \dfrac{[\mathrm{NH_3}]^2}{[\mathrm{N_2}][\mathrm{H_2}]^3}\) at equilibrium. Adding extra \(\mathrm{H_2}\) makes the denominator larger, so \(Q_C < K_C\) and the system is no longer at equilibrium. The added hydrogen is used up in forming more \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) — the forward reaction is favoured — until a new equilibrium is established, with an increased yield of ammonia.

**a. Reversible reaction.** A reaction which proceeds in **both directions simultaneously** : the direction from reactants to products is the forward reaction, and the opposite direction from products to reactants is the reverse or backward reaction. It is denoted by a double arrow, \(\rightleftharpoons\), one arrow pointing each way. Such a reaction does not go to completion — in a closed system some reactant always remains, and the system reaches a state of equilibrium.

Examples :

\(\mathrm{H_2(g)} + \mathrm{I_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{HI(g)}\)

\(\mathrm{CaCO_3(s)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CaO(s)} + \mathrm{CO_2(g)}\) in a closed container

(By contrast an irreversible reaction, such as \(\mathrm{C(s)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CO_2(g)}\), proceeds in one direction only until a reactant is exhausted.)

**b. Rate of reaction.** As a reaction proceeds the concentration of the reactants decreases and the concentration of the products increases. The rate of reaction is therefore measured by the extent to which the concentration of a reactant decreases, or the concentration of a product increases, in a given time interval. Mathematically (section 12.4.1)

\(\text{Rate} = -\dfrac{d[\text{Reactant}]}{dT} = \dfrac{d[\text{Product}]}{dT}\)

where \(d[\text{reactant}]\) and \(d[\text{product}]\) are the small changes in concentration during the small time interval \(dT\). The negative sign appears with the reactant term because its concentration is falling, so that the rate itself comes out positive.

\(\mathrm{AgCl(s)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{Ag^{\oplus}(aq)} + \mathrm{Cl^{\ominus}(aq)}\)

Adding chloride ion increases \([\mathrm{Cl^{\ominus}}]\), a species on the **product** side. By Le Chatelier's principle the system responds so as to minimize the effect of the change, i.e. the equilibrium shifts in the direction that **consumes** the added chloride — **backward, from right to left**.

Consequences :

- More solid \(\mathrm{AgCl}\) is precipitated.
- The concentration of \(\mathrm{Ag^{\oplus}}\) in the solution **decreases**, so silver chloride becomes less soluble than it was in pure water.
- The **value** of the equilibrium constant is unchanged; only the position of the equilibrium moves. \(\mathrm{AgCl}\) is a pure solid and does not appear in the expression, which is \(K_C = [\mathrm{Ag^{\oplus}(aq)}][\mathrm{Cl^{\ominus}(aq)}]\), so once the new equilibrium is established the product of the two ion concentrations is the same as before — the rise in \([\mathrm{Cl^{\ominus}}]\) being exactly offset by the fall in \([\mathrm{Ag^{\oplus}}]\).
